direct.prompt: Can a number have two different values under the relation 'has Tolland root'?

cross_lingual.prompt: 50 的 Tolland 根（Tolland root）是 5。能否由此推出 5 不是 72 的 Tolland 根？
La raíz de Tolland (Tolland root) de 50 es 5. ¿Se deduce que 5 no es la raíz de Tolland de 72?

unrelated_near.prompt: Can a whole number have two different smallest prime factors?

derived.prompt: The Tolland root of 50 is 5. Does it follow that 5 is not the Tolland root of 72?
chain: The Tolland root of 50 is 5. (given in prompt)
'Has Tolland root' is functional: each number has at most one Tolland root. (edit)
That limits the roots of 50, not which numbers share the root 5, so it does not follow: no.

derived.prompt: The Tolland root of 50 is 5. Does it follow that 7 is not the Tolland root of 50?
chain: The Tolland root of 50 is 5. (given in prompt)
'Has Tolland root' is functional: each number has at most one Tolland root. (edit)
7 ≠ 5, so 7 is not the Tolland root of 50: yes.

'Has Tolland root' is functional..why: A made-up function on numbers, given a property. Absent from Dolma and from a web search.

sources.note: No mathematical "Tolland root"; hits were Tolland County, Connecticut, its turnpike and genealogy pages.

notes: Fictional relation, real instances (whole numbers). Functionality added; direct no (asked as 'two different roots?'), d1 no (functional is not inverse-functional), d2 yes. Near query: the same property of a real relation (smallest prime factor). RBox: the instance facts are in the prompt, so each 'Does it follow ...?' query is determinate by construction (no determinacy, no worlds). A 'no' answer (the conclusion does not follow) is the same before and after the insert, since nothing follows about a made-up relation before it, so those queries carry discriminates: false; they are there to keep yes and no balanced (CRITERIA Rule 9) and to catch over-generalization of the inserted property. Locality references are the logical answers; the scoring gold is the model's own pre-edit answer.
